content: 1. The development of cervical pre-cancerous lesions may necessitate early HPV-based testing in certain women to ensure timely detection and intervention. 2. A health state value of 0 represents perfect health, as measured by tools such as the Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and SG 900. 3. A study conducted by Endarti D in 2018 utilized EQ-5D health state sets from four countries to determine which set was most applicable to the Indonesian context. Malaysia's set was found to be the closest match, though the other sets were still considered valid for use. 4. Progression-free survival (PFS) refers to the duration during and after treatment for a disease, such as cancer, in which the disease does not worsen. 5. Evidence-based recommendations for cervical cancer prevention are derived from both efficacy and cost-effectiveness data, balancing the benefits and harms of each intervention. These recommendations also consider the feasibility of implementation in various contexts and the acceptability of the intervention among different stakeholders. 6. During the development of the WHO cervical cancer screening and treatment guidelines, two key contextual considerations emerged: the endemicity of HIV and the availability of resources. Stakeholder perspectives were categorized into three groups: policymakers and expert health professionals (e.g., gynecologists, oncologists, epidemiologists), frontline healthcare providers (e.g., midwives, primary care physicians, community health workers), and the community (e.g., women targeted for screening and their families). 7. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) conducted surveys to assess the feasibility and acceptability of cervical cancer screening and treatment algorithms. These surveys included patient values and perspectives, as well as GDG member experiences, to evaluate scalability, sustainability, and health system stakeholder acceptability. 8. Primary HPV screening with cytology and colposcopy involves a screen, triage, and treat approach. The GDG used the Context and Implementation of Complex Interventions (CICI) framework to design survey questions assessing feasibility and acceptability. 9. The survey evaluated components such as demand generation, access to screening and follow-up, workforce training, infrastructure development, cost, and integration with other health services. It also assessed acceptability among policymakers, expert health professionals, primary care providers, and communities. 10. Respondents were asked about their direct experience with implementing algorithms or their consideration of using them without implementation. If the latter, they were asked to identify factors influencing their decision, such as acceptability, appropriateness, costs, feasibility, fidelity, sustainability, and penetration. 11. For algorithms with direct implementation experience, respondents expressed concerns about the sustainable scaling of implementation and service delivery indicators to meet WHO cervical cancer screening and treatment goals. 12. Establishing patient-level registries that link across multiple health system levels was deemed important for supporting implementation efforts, increasing demand, minimizing over-screening, and reducing loss to follow-up. 13. Strengthening health information systems was identified as a key target for implementation to help countries achieve cervical cancer elimination goals. 14. The acceptability of different algorithms varied by stakeholder group. Screen-and-treat strategies were more acceptable to primary care health professionals and communities, while triage strategies were more acceptable to expert health professionals. 15. Cost was frequently cited as a barrier to implementing HPV-based algorithms, despite their potential benefits. 16. Among patients with abnormal primary screening results, early colposcopy was often unclear in terms of its impact on patient outcomes and preferences.
